step1_summary: Chief complaint: Sudden-onset dizziness/vertigo (“room is spinning”) with nausea.

Symptom details: • Started ≈2 h prior while making breakfast; continuous since onset. • Similar brief episode 1 mo ago (5–10 min). • Associated ear buzzing/tinnitus. • Feels unsteady but no true limb weakness. • No vomiting yet, no headache, no ear pain/discharge, no recent viral illness, no fever.
Past medical history: Premature ovarian failure; on hormone-replacement therapy (HRT). No other chronic diseases noted.
Medications/allergies: HRT; no other regular meds. Denies drug allergies.
Family/social history: Married; no other details reported (smoking, alcohol, vascular risk factors not discussed).
Vital signs/exam: Video visit only; vitals not measured. Patient reports intact motor strength, able to ambulate but veers because of vertigo. No focal neuro deficits elicited.
Labs/imaging: None performed or mentioned during visit.

V: Cerebellar or vertebrobasilar ischemic stroke/TIA: acute vertigo with gait unsteadiness could reflect posterior-circulation event, especially if continuous.
Vertebral artery dissection: can present with acute vertigo in younger patients without classic risk factors.
I: Vestibular neuritis / viral labyrinthitis: inflammation of vestibular nerve/inner ear causes hours–days of vertigo, nausea, tinnitus.
Acute otitis media/interna: middle/inner-ear infection may give vertigo, although ear pain/discharge are absent.
N: Vestibular schwannoma (acoustic neuroma): progressive tinnitus ± episodic vertigo, though typically chronic.
D: Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV): otolith degeneration causes vertigo often seconds–minutes with head movement.
Age-related cervical spondylosis causing vertebrobasilar insufficiency on rotation.
I2: Drug-induced vertigo (e.g., ototoxic meds, alcohol): not likely—no offending agents reported.
HRT-related thrombotic event (rare) leading to stroke/TIA.
C: Congenital semicircular-canal malformation: usually lifelong history, unlikely new at age 42.
A: Ménière’s disease (autoimmune inner-ear hydrops): recurrent vertigo, tinnitus, hearing fluctuation.
Multiple sclerosis: demyelinating lesions can cause acute vestibular syndrome.
T: Post-traumatic vestibulopathy/concussion: no recent head injury reported.
E: Hypoglycemia: can cause dizziness, shakiness, nausea.
Anemia: nonspecific dizziness; unlikely to cause true spinning vertigo.

step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Classic acute vestibular syndrome with continuous spinning vertigo, nausea, tinnitus, gait unsteadiness, and no focal neurologic deficits fits vestibular neuritis/labyrinthitis best.
Recurrent episodes (prior 5-10 min event; current longer) plus tinnitus are compatible, though absence of fluctuating hearing loss and longer current episode make it less likely.
Very common cause of vertigo; however attacks are usually brief (<1 min) and triggered by position changes, which patient does not report. Still considered because of age and prior transient episode.
Acute persistent vertigo with imbalance could signal cerebellar ischemia; lack of focal deficits lowers probability but does not exclude, especially without exam/vitals.
Shakiness and dizziness can occur, but true spinning vertigo is uncommon; no diabetes or medication risk noted.

supporting_evidence: Sudden onset continuous spinning vertigo lasting hours
No focal limb weakness or other neurologic deficits
opposing_evidence: No hearing loss (labyrinthitis often has hearing loss, though vestibular neuritis does not)
No documented fluctuating or reduced hearing
Current episode longer than typical 20 min–12 h Ménière’s range but prior was very short

supporting_evidence: Prior very brief vertigo spell could represent BPPV
opposing_evidence: Current vertigo is continuous and not clearly positional
No mention of symptom provocation with head movement

supporting_evidence: Acute persistent vertigo with gait unsteadiness
opposing_evidence: Age 42 with no vascular risk factors mentioned
No focal neuro findings, no headache, no vomiting
No diabetes, insulin, or sulfonylurea use
